title: Clarity Is What Creates Speed
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Uses a Formula One pit crew's two-second tire change as a model for what real speed requires: not urgency, but clarity about who owns what and in what sequence, rehearsed until no hesitation exists. Contrasts this with the common leadership mistake of applying pressure and micromanaging in the name of urgency, which the piece argues creates motion and conflict but not actual speed. Distills the pit crew model into concrete practices -- single-owner tasks, a fixed sequence, rehearsal as the real work, contingency planning, and autonomous execution once the plan is set -- as directly transferable to workplace teams.
points: Speed comes from removing every question about who does what before the moment arrives, not from applying pressure or urgency.
Every task should have exactly one owner -- 'when everyone is responsible, no one is' -- with a fixed, rehearsed sequence rather than improvisation.
Rehearsal is itself the work: dry runs where team members articulate ownership and handoffs in advance are what make execution fast when it counts.
quotes: A Formula One pit crew changes four tires, adjusts the front wing, and sends a car back onto the track in two seconds. Two seconds.
The fastest way to move together is to remove every question about who does what before the moment arrives.
Urgency without clarity creates motion, confusion, and conflict. But it can’t create speed.
Every task has exactly one person responsible. Not the team or a subset. One person. When everyone is responsible, no one is.
The takeaway for workplace teams is clear-cut. When execution speed suffers, the team doesn’t have an urgency problem. It has a clarity problem.
